name: vestibular paroxysmia
aliases: neurovascular cross-compression of the eighth nerve
microvascular compression syndrome of cranial nerve VIII

reference.source: Bárány Society diagnostic criteria for vestibular paroxysmia
clinicalPearls: The hallmark is short, recurrent, stereotyped spells of spinning or non-spinning vertigo lasting seconds to under a minute, which may occur many times a day.
It is attributed to pulsatile neurovascular cross-compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve, mechanistically analogous to trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm.
Attacks may arise spontaneously or be provoked by particular head positions or by hyperventilation, and may be accompanied by transient unilateral tinnitus or a change in hearing.
A clear response to low doses of a sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant (such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine) supports the diagnosis and is one of the formal diagnostic criteria.

High-resolution heavily T2-weighted MRI (CISS or FIESTA) may show a vessel, most often the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, looping onto the nerve, but such contact is frequent in asymptomatic people, so imaging is supportive rather than diagnostic.
Between attacks the examination is usually normal, although some patients develop a mild progressive vestibular or cochlear deficit over time.
Hyperventilation-induced nystagmus may be demonstrable and is a useful bedside clue.
The condition must be distinguished from benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular migraine, Menière's disease, and panic attacks before treatment is committed.
reference.pathophysiology: Vestibular paroxysmia is caused by pulsatile compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve by an adjacent artery — most often the anterior inferior cerebellar artery — at or near the root entry zone, where central oligodendrocyte myelin transitions to peripheral Schwann-cell myelin and the nerve is especially vulnerable. Chronic mechanical irritation produces focal demyelination, which permits ephaptic (cross-talk) transmission between axons and generates paroxysmal ectopic and self-sustaining discharges. These brief bursts of abnormal afferent activity are perceived as short, stereotyped attacks of vertigo, exactly analogous to the paroxysms of trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm arising from compression of neighbouring cranial nerves. Membrane-stabilising, sodium-channel-blocking drugs suppress this ectopic firing, which accounts for their characteristic therapeutic effect.
additionalDifferentials: superior semicircular canal dehiscence or perilymph fistula
additionalInvestigations: high-resolution heavily T2-weighted MRI (CISS/FIESTA) with MR angiography of the cerebellopontine angle
pure-tone audiometry to detect an associated cochlear deficit or exclude other causes
video head impulse testing, caloric testing, and vestibular evoked myogenic potentials
bedside hyperventilation testing for provoked nystagmus
positional testing to exclude benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
a monitored therapeutic trial of a sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant
redFlags: progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss suggesting a vestibular schwannoma or other cerebellopontine angle tumour
facial weakness, facial numbness, or additional cranial neuropathies
signs of brainstem ischaemia such as dysarthria, diplopia, or limb ataxia
papilloedema or other features of raised intracranial pressure
failure to respond to an adequate trial of a sodium-channel-blocking drug, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The disorder usually responds well to sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsants, often at low doses, with a marked reduction in attack frequency; medically refractory cases may be considered for microvascular decompression, though some patients show slow progression of vestibulocochlear deficit.
pitfalls: over-diagnosing the condition on the basis of incidental neurovascular contact seen on MRI in an asymptomatic person
confusing brief positional attacks with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo or with vestibular migraine
treating a therapeutic response as definitive proof, since other paroxysmal disorders may also respond
neglecting to exclude a cerebellopontine angle tumour before attributing symptoms to vascular compression
escalating medication without re-examining the diagnosis when attacks fail to remit
